answers.text: Because the refill is computed from elapsed time on each call, the bucket never needs a timer: idle time is credited lazily the next time take() runs, capped at capacity so a long idle period cannot bank an unlimited burst.
Fractions work because the regular expression accepts an optional decimal part and the result is rounded to whole milliseconds, so 1.5h becomes 5,400,000 ms.

steps.summary: parseDuration only accepts seconds. Replace the single-unit regex with a unit table so new units are data, not new branches, and validate the result.

parseDuration now accepts ms, s, m and h (including fractions like 1.5h) and rejects zero or unknown units. Tests pass.

walkthrough.title: Durations become a lookup, not a special case

remember.note: parseDuration uses a unit table (ms, s, m, h) instead of one regex per unit.
Explained lookup tables replacing branches; no need to explain the pattern again.

walkthrough.summary: parseDuration now converts any supported unit through one table and rejects values that would schedule nothing.

terms.name: unit table
terms.meaning: maps a unit suffix to milliseconds

narration.text: Before this change, parseDuration matched exactly one shape: a number followed by s.
Anything like five minutes was rejected, so schedules had to be written in seconds.
The idea is simple: every unit is just a multiplier into milliseconds.
So the unit table stores those multipliers, and adding a unit means adding one entry, not another branch.

scenes.label: Implementation
scenes.title: One pattern, one lookup, one guard

narration.text: The pattern now captures an amount, which may have a decimal part, and one of four unit suffixes.
The amount is multiplied by the unit table entry.
Finally, a guard rejects zero or non-finite results, because a zero-length schedule would fire continuously.

scenes.label: Evidence
scenes.title: Tests pin the new units and the edge cases

narration.text: The new tests cover minutes, hours and a fractional value.
They also check that zero and an unknown unit are rejected, and the test run in this turn passed.

# ledger-api

A small sample project used to demonstrate Active walkthroughs.

steps.summary: Bursts of balance and transaction calls trigger 429s. A token bucket lets short bursts through and paces the rest; on 429 we should honor Retry-After by pausing the shared limiter.

steps.text: I'll add a token-bucket limiter, route every request through it, and handle 429 Retry-After.

steps.summary: Retrying on 429 recursively is fine because pauseFor drains the bucket, so the retry waits for Retry-After before taking a token.

steps.text: Requests now go through a shared token bucket (burst 5, 2/s). A 429 pauses the bucket for Retry-After and retries. Tests are running in the background.

walkthrough.title: A token bucket paces the ledger client
walkthrough.summary: Every request now takes a token from a shared bucket that refills over time; a 429 response drains it and pauses for Retry-After.

terms.name: token bucket
terms.meaning: a counter of request permits that refills at a fixed rate up to a capacity

scenes.label: The problem
scenes.title: Bursts of calls hit the API's limit

narration.text: When a screen loads, it can fire many balance and transaction calls at once, and the ledger API answers some of them with 429, too many requests.
The fix puts a token bucket between every caller and the network.
Requests flow on at a steady pace, and a 429 sends a pause signal back to the bucket.

scenes.label: Underlying concept
scenes.title: Tokens refill with elapsed time, up to a cap

narration.text: The token bucket is one number that grows with time.
Each refill adds elapsed seconds times the refill rate, and never exceeds the capacity, so idle time can't bank an unlimited burst.

scenes.label: Implementation
scenes.title: take() waits exactly long enough for one token

narration.text: If a whole token is available, take spends it and returns immediately. That is the burst.
Otherwise it computes how long until the missing fraction refills, sleeps that long, and tries again.

scenes.label: Behavior
scenes.title: Five fast requests, then two per second

visual.title: Wait before each of 8 back-to-back requests (capacity 5, 2 per second)

narration.text: Here's an example with the client's defaults, capacity five and two tokens per second. This is worked out from the code, not measured.
The first five requests go straight through; after that, each one waits about half a second.

scenes.label: Code diff
scenes.title: Every call now goes through request()

narration.text: In the client, a new request method takes a token before every fetch.
On a 429 it reads Retry-After, pauses the shared bucket, and retries; getBalance and listTransactions both route through it.

scenes.label: Tradeoffs
scenes.title: Pausing the bucket protects every caller

narration.text: pauseFor drains the bucket and blocks takes until the server's Retry-After has passed, so one 429 slows every caller instead of letting them all retry at once.
The tradeoff is that the retry has no attempt limit, so a server that keeps answering 429 keeps the call waiting.
